To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) TSNA-induced DNA damage is a necessary, but insufficient, prerequisite for cancer induction, and (ii) that the TSNA-induced DNA-damage in oral snuff users is not sufficient to explain the high cancer risk.
TSNA-induced DNA damage in humans is insignificant.

1) TSNA induced DNA adduct levels in humans are orders of magnitude below those predicted from animal experiments; 2) TSNA-induced DNA adducts in humans are not detectable by the current methodology; 3) the observed TSNA-induced increment in the background level of POB-hemoglobin adducts in exposed individuals is consistent with the predictions from animal experiments; and 4) the high background levels of DNA adducts are not caused by TSNA
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the molecular basis for induction and progression of human cancers by TSNA.

i) the molecular basis for induction by tobacco specific nitrosoamines of human cancers of the oral cavity and pharynx, and ii) the extrapolation from animals to humans of TSNA induced cellular DNA damage.
the elucidation of the molecular basis for TSNA induced human cancer and the development of methods for the early detection of TSNA-induced cancers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of low nitrosamine oral snuff is "safe", and the use of high nitrosamine oral tobacco snuff is "not safe".
TSNA-induced DNA adducts are not causally related to cancer in humans, at least not in low-nitrosamines oral snuff users.
the TSNA exposure from oral snuff use does not increase the risk for cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TSNA-induced carcinogenic effects in humans can be predicted from animal data, but only for exposures that exceed the background level of endogenous DNA damage.
the use of low TSNA containing tobacco products is safe.
the human exposure to TSNA is not negligible, but that it does not contribute to the background level of DNA adducts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the TSNA exposure from the use of oral snuffs with low concentrations of nitrosamines, is not sufficient to cause DNA damage that is not already present at a background level.
TSNA-induced carcinogenesis is highly unlikely to occur at the low TSNA levels present in oral snuffs.
the TSNA induced cancer risk in humans from oral snuffs is not significantly different from the risk in rodents.
